extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant), especially those studying teleology and the Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and maxims from Kant's discussion of teleological judgement: definitions and regulative rules for judging organised natural beings, the distinction between reflective and determinant judgement, and classificatory schemes for systems that explain purposiveness in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of internal purposiveness (definition of organised being)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised product of nature is one in which every part is reciprocally purpose and means. In it nothing is vain, without purpose, or to be ascribed to a blind mechanism of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle serves as a definition and maxim for judging internal purposiveness in organised beings; dissectors and observers tacitly assume that 'nothing in such a creature is vain' when investigating structure and function. It is presented as empirically occasioned but requiring an a priori regulative status (a maxim) because of the universality and necessity ascribed to such purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: teleological judgement as regulative, not constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of purposiveness in nature is not a constitutive concept of Understanding or Reason but can serve as a regulative concept for reflective Judgement to guide investigation by analogy with our own purposive causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Idea of purposiveness as a guiding heuristic (maxim) for reflection and investigation, not as an objective claim about natural causes; it helps form hypotheses and direct observation but does not license asserting a distinct ontological kind of cause without further metaphysical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer natural purpose from mere external utility
rubrics_metrics.description: External purposiveness (usefulness to other beings or contingent relations) does not suffice to judge something a purpose of nature; internal organisation is what affords objective reality to the concept of a 'purpose of nature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rivers, mountains, slopes, or plants useful to humans should not be judged categorically as natural purposes solely because of external utility; for a thing to be a natural purpose one must consider its internal form and organisation (e.g., a blade of grass as internally purposive). External relations can only yield hypothetical/purposive judgements, not categorical ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: organised matter implies natural purpose leading to idea of nature as system
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as matter is organised it necessarily carries with it the concept of a natural purpose because its specific form is a product of nature; this leads to the Idea of collective nature as a system according to the rule of purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a regulative maxim for reflective judgement: from the fact of internal organisation we may heuristically posit nature-as-system and extend teleological investigation to study natural phenomena as if subordinated to a purposive order (without thereby proving designedness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit teleology within natural science; avoid theological domestication
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science must not introduce the concept of God as an internal (domestic) principle to explain purposiveness; doing so mixes foreign (theological) principles with the principles of physics and produces circularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological explanations are to be kept as regulative for reflective investigation in natural science. Introducing a supernatural Author as a domestic explanatory principle creates a delusive circle (using teleology to prove God and God to ground teleology) and undermines the internal consistency of the sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as a methodological mode, not an internal constitutive principle of Physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological judgement is admissible as a method for investigating certain classes of natural objects (especially organised beings) but is not an internal constitutive principle of Physics; arithmetic, geometry, or universal mechanical laws, though strikingly unified, are not teleological grounds for physical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleology to supplement mechanical explanation where mechanical laws are inadequate to account for organisation, but do not substitute teleological principles for empirically grounded mechanical laws in constitutive physical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between determinant and reflective judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinant Judgement subsumes under given laws or concepts and has no autonomy; reflective Judgement must subsume under a law not yet given and therefore operates with necessary maxims and may be exposed to antinomies between such maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which mode of judgement is in play: do not treat maxims appropriate to reflective judgement as determinant (objective) principles. Confusing the two leads to antinomy and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: First maxim of reflective judgement (mechanical maxim)
rubrics_metrics.description: All production of material things and their forms must be judged to be possible according to merely mechanical laws (as a guiding thread for investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim directs us to investigate nature via mechanical explanations wherever possible; it is a regulative demand for thorough empirical inquiry, not a denial that other modes of reflection might be used when mechanical explanation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second maxim of reflective judgement (teleological maxim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some products of material nature cannot be judged to be possible according to merely mechanical laws; to judge them requires a different law of causality, namely that of final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim counsels that, in certain cases (notably organised beings), we are compelled by our cognitive situation to reflect in terms of final causes as an idea guiding investigation; again, this is a regulative move, not an assertion of an objective metaphysical final-cause causality for determinant judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting regulative maxims into constitutive principles (solution to the antinomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent antinomy between the mechanistic and teleological maxims arises from confusing reflective (regulative) propositions with determinant (constitutive) ones; we cannot prove the impossibility of organisation by mechanism nor prove design as an objective principle—each belongs to distinct legislative roles of judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the autonomy of reflective judgement: treat teleological ideas as heuristics for inquiry while continuing mechanical investigation; do not assert teleological causality as an objective law for determinant judgement without transcending possible empirical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of explanatory systems about purposiveness (Technic of Nature: Idealism vs Realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems explaining purposiveness split into Idealism (purposiveness is undesigned—either casual or fatalistic) and Realism (some purposiveness is designed—either physical/hylozoism or hyperphysical/theism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating accounts of purposiveness, distinguish whether they (a) deny intentionality and explain purposiveness as chance or necessity, (b) ascribe purposiveness to life in matter (hylozoism), or (c) ascribe it to an intelligent original ground (theism). Each option has different implications and problems; the discussion warns that none of these systems fully accomplishes what they promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technica distinction: designed vs undesigned purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Technic' (productive causality) of nature can be divided into 'designed' (technica intentionalis) — where purposiveness is the result of intention — and 'undesigned' (technica naturalis) — where purposiveness is at bottom similar to mechanism and is a subjective condition of judging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to evaluate explanatory claims: do they posit genuine design (intentional causality) or reduce purposiveness to an appearance grounded in contingent agreement with human concepts? Beware conflating the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical standard: objections to chance and ontological unity explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts that explain purposiveness by blind chance (Epicurean) or by collapsing contingency into an ontological subsistence (Spinozism) fail to explain purposive unity: blind chance explains nothing and subsistence-in-subject removes contingency and design, thereby failing to produce a unity of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing theories of purposiveness, require that they actually account for purposive reference (unity of purpose grounded in understanding) rather than invoking chance or ontological subsistence which do not yield purposive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of teleological examples as heuristic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete phenomena (e.g., grass for oxen, tapeworms prompting cleanliness, mosquitoes prompting drainage, dreams as remedial for sleep, beauty as relation to free play of faculties) illustrate how teleological judgement can inform understanding of natural forms and their role in a possible system of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such examples to test and flesh out teleological hypotheses about internal purposiveness, while remembering their role as illustrative/regulative rather than constitutive proof of design.
